In game: the pause button opens the port menu.
Wario Land: Shake It! running natively, not emulated.
Your copy of the game is not here yet.
This port contains nothing from the game. Game data explains how to put your own copy on this phone.

The D-pad is on the left, 1, 2 and A on the right, SHAKE for Wario\'s shake, and + and − at the top. Tilting the phone tilts the Wii Remote and shaking the phone shakes it. A Bluetooth gamepad works too.
How the game fills your screen.
16:9 and Fill make the game itself draw wider, so there is more of the level at the sides.

New in this port: removes the side panels the game frames its 4:3 play area with, so the level fills the screen — something the original never did. Only with 16:9, Fill or Cinematic, and it applies when the game starts.
Phones compose every frame anyway, so turning this off rarely changes what you see.
The game is drawn at this height and then scaled to the screen. Above 1080p a phone GPU usually costs more frames than it gains looks.

Draws fewer pixels while a scene is too heavy for the GPU — a boss shaking the screen, a room full of effects — instead of dropping to 30 frames, and gives them back as soon as the scene lets up. The resolution above stays the most it will ever draw.
Vulkan, always: it is the only graphics API this engine has on Android.
Works around drivers that draw the game wrong. Automatic turns it on for the GPUs known to need it, which is most phone GPUs.
Experimental. The game still runs at 60; the frames between are made up. Each one draws the scene again, so on a phone this costs battery and heat for little gain.
Keeps the sound steady when the game thread is busy. Turn it off only to test whether it is causing a problem.
Automatic follows the phone. The disc carries English, Spanish and French.
The game only reads a Wii Remote held sideways, so that is what it is given.
D-pad on the left; 1, 2 and A on the right; SHAKE for Wario\'s shake; + and − at the top. Touches that miss every button reach the game\'s own menus.
The phone becomes the Wii Remote: turn it to tilt, shake it to shake. The on-screen buttons keep working at the same time.
Aims up to 85° in the direction you push, as on PC. L1 and R1 tilt by 30°, L2 and R2 shake.
Rarely needed, and easy to get wrong.
Reads higher-resolution textures from the Textures folder in the app\'s data folder.
Writes every texture the game uses, to make a pack from. It fills storage quickly; leave it off while playing.
Skip shaders that are not compiled yet
Keeps the game moving instead of stopping for each new shader; something may be missing for a frame or two. On a phone this is worth having.
The Wii blurred the image slightly as it scanned it out. Off is sharper but not what the game looked like.
Your own copy of the disc. Nothing from the game ships with this port.
Reading that folder needs all-files access, because the engine opens the disc as a path rather than through the document picker. It is only ever used to read the game.

You need Wario Land: Shake It! (USA, RWLE01, revision 0). Pick the disc image below (.iso, .wbfs, .rvz, .wia, .gcz or .ciso) and the app extracts it here — about 3.5 GB, and the image itself is read where it is, not copied. You can also extract it on a PC with Dolphin (Properties, Filesystem, right-click the disc, Extract Entire Disc) and copy the folder to the path above.
If you would rather pick the folder here, it is copied into %1$s, which needs room for a second copy.
